title: The rock cycle
keyIdea: Rock is always changing, very slowly, from one kind to another. Weathering breaks rock at the surface into bits, and erosion carries them away. The bits settle in layers and are pressed and glued into sedimentary rock. Heat and squeezing deep underground change rock into metamorphic rock without melting it. Rock that melts becomes magma, and magma cools into igneous rock. The loop has no start, and any kind of rock can take a short cut to any other kind.
familyTip: On a walk, look at old walls, gravestones or pebbles. Ask: what is breaking this rock down, and where will the bits go? Pebbles on a beach are bits of rock that were rubbed smooth on the way.

visual.caption: Where does it happen? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: weather rocks into a river, follow a grain round the loop, find short cuts, place each change, sort fast from slow.

kid: There are three kinds of rock. Igneous rock forms when melted rock cools and goes hard. Sedimentary rock forms from layers of sand, mud or shells that are pressed together. Metamorphic rock forms when rock is heated and squeezed deep underground, but does not melt.

At the surface, rain, ice and wind break rock into bits. This is called weathering. Then rivers, ice and wind carry the bits away. This is called erosion. The bits settle in layers, often on the sea floor. New layers press down on old ones, and minerals in the water glue the grains. That makes new sedimentary rock.

Deep underground, rock gets hot and squeezed. If it does not melt, it turns into metamorphic rock. If it gets hot enough to melt, it becomes magma. When magma cools, it turns into igneous rock again. So rock goes round and round. We call this the rock cycle.

The rock cycle has no start and no end. Rock can also take short cuts. Any kind of rock can be worn into bits, changed by heat, or melted. Most of these changes take thousands or millions of years, so we only see a tiny part of them.
adult: Ages 9 to 11. This builds on the three rock types and leads into the KS3 rock cycle. Key words: weathering, erosion, deposition, compaction, cementation, heat and pressure, melting, magma, lava, cooling, crystals and uplift.

The facts follow the British Geological Survey and the Geological Society. Weathering breaks rock down where it is, and erosion moves the bits. Compaction and cementation turn sediment into sedimentary rock. Heat and pressure change solid rock without melting it. Magma that cools slowly underground grows large crystals, and lava that cools fast at the surface has tiny ones. Uplift brings deep rock back up, where it can be weathered.

Common mistakes: thinking the cycle has a fixed start, or that rock must go round it in order; mixing up heat and pressure with melting; mixing up weathering with erosion; calling magma igneous rock before it has cooled; and thinking new rock forms in a few years. Be careful with diagrams that show one neat circle, because real rock takes many short cuts.

In the lab your child cracks granite, sandstone and marble and sends the bits down a river to make layers. They pick the process at each stop as a grain of quartz goes right round the loop. Then they find three short cuts, put five changes in their places in a slice through the ground, and sort six changes into fast and slow.

practice.prompt: Which process turns loose sand on the sea floor into sandstone?
practice.hint: Think about what happens to layers that pile up for a long time.
practice.explain: Compaction and cementation. The weight of new layers squeezes the sand, and minerals glue the grains into rock.

practice.prompt: Mud settles on a lake floor at {a} mm each year. How many millimetres of mud settle in 100 years?
practice.hint: Multiply the amount each year by the number of years.
practice.explain: {a} mm each year for 100 years is {=a*100} mm. That is only {=a*10} cm, so thick layers take a very long time.

practice.prompt: Shale is buried deep, where it is heated and squeezed until it changes into slate. It never melts. What kind of rock is slate?
practice.hint: Did the rock melt? If not, which kind of rock forms?
practice.explain: Metamorphic. Heat and squeezing without melting change rock into metamorphic rock.

practice.prompt: A cliff shows {a} layers of sandstone. Each layer took about 1,000 years to build up. About how many years did all the layers take?
practice.hint: Each layer is about 1,000 years. Multiply by the number of layers.
practice.explain: {a} layers × 1,000 years is about {=a*1000} years. Rock layers record long stretches of time.

practice.prompt: Granite is igneous rock. Which of these can happen to it next?
choices: Any of these: weathering, heating or melting
Nothing: it stays granite for ever
practice.hint: Remember the short cuts. Is granite stuck on one path?
practice.explain: Any of them. Granite at the surface can be weathered, and buried granite can be changed by heat or melted. Rock can take many paths.

pool.prompt: What is the difference between weathering and erosion?
choices: Weathering breaks rock; erosion carries the bits away
Weathering carries the bits; erosion breaks rock
pool.hint: One happens where the rock stands. The other moves things.
pool.explain: Weathering breaks rock into bits where it stands. Erosion is when water, ice or wind carry the bits away.

pool.prompt: Where does the rock cycle begin?
choices: It has no start: it is a loop
pool.hint: Can you find a first step on a loop?
pool.explain: It has no start. The rock cycle is a loop, and rock can join or leave it at any point.

pool.prompt: Sand settles on a sea floor at {a} mm each year. How many millimetres settle in {b} years?
pool.hint: Multiply the yearly amount by the number of years.
pool.explain: {a} mm × {b} years = {=a*b} mm. Even after many years, the layer is still thin.

pool.prompt: Magma cools slowly, deep underground. What does it form?
pool.hint: Slow cooling gives crystals more time to grow.
pool.explain: Igneous rock with big crystals, like granite. Slow cooling gives the crystals time to grow.

pool.prompt: Marble is pushed up to the surface and weathered. What can the bits become in the end?
pool.hint: What happens to sediment that is buried under new layers?
pool.explain: Sedimentary rock. The bits become sediment, which is pressed and glued into new rock. Marble took a short cut.

pool.prompt: Which change is fast enough to watch?
pool.hint: Most of the rock cycle is very slow. Which one takes seconds?
pool.explain: A rockfall takes seconds. Making sandstone or marble takes thousands to millions of years.

pool.prompt: Lava pours out of a volcano and cools quickly in the air. What forms?
pool.hint: Lava is melted rock. What forms when melted rock cools, and how fast was it?
pool.explain: Igneous rock with tiny crystals, like basalt. Fast cooling leaves no time for big crystals.

pool.prompt: A riverbank is worn back {a} cm each year. How many centimetres does it lose in {b} years?
pool.hint: Multiply the amount lost each year by the number of years.
pool.explain: {a} cm × {b} years = {=a*b} cm. Erosion is slow, but it adds up over time.
